newsitem.title: UK: Blair says Britain unlikely to join EMU first wave.
newsitem.headline: Blair says Britain unlikely to join EMU first wave.

text.p: Tony Blair, who could well be Britain's new Labour Prime Minister in three weeks' time, said on Thursday it was "highly unlikely" he would take the country into a European single currency in 1999.

Distancing his party further from a project for which most Britons show little enthusiasm, Blair said the decision on whether to join should not be based on political considerations, but purely on economic ones.

Blair's foreign affairs spokesman Robin Cook said last week that if Britain missed the single currency bus in 1999, it would be unlikely to join during the course of the five-year parliament which Britons will elect on May 1.
"In principle there are advantages which could come from a single currency," Blair told pupils at a school in Redditch, central England during a campaign trip.
"But it has got to be economically right for Britain and it should not be politically driven...I think it is highly unlikely we would be in the first wave."

Labour is traditionally seen as a party more friendly to Brussels than the Conservatives, who have ruled Britain since 1979. But under Blair, Labour's approach to a single currency is very similar to the Conservatives'.

One key difference between the two parties is that Blair is committed, for instance, to signing up to the European Union's Social Chapter on workplace rights, and to implementing EU rules limiting working time.

But Blair warned Britain's European partners that it would be dangerous to go ahead with a single currency without the necessary close convergence between the performance of the economies of the participating countries.
"It is a very big step and unless the economies fit together properly, it could do very real damage," Blair said.

Labour leads by between 15 and 23 points in the opinion polls three weeks ahead of the election, making it odds on that Blair will be prime minister when the crucial decisions on a single currency are taken later this year.
He said that whether or not Britain joined the project, it was important that it should remain in the negotiations to agree how the currency would operate.

This is a point which has been repeatedly emphasised by Prime Minister John Major in his battle with so-called Conservative "Eurosceptics" who fear that Brussels is trying to subsume Britain into a federal superstate.
"The single currency, if it goes ahead, is going to affect this country whether we are in or out. It is very important that we keep our place at the negotiating table," Blair said.
